sentences: Here Jeong Seon, also known as Gyeomjae, compresses the whole of Mount Geumgang into a single round mass, as if in a bird's-eye view from the sky.
Its twelve thousand peaks are gathered onto one sheet of paper more than 130 centimetres tall.
Jeong Seon first travelled to Mount Geumgang in the autumn of 1711, and he kept returning to it in his art for decades.
No one could see this view from one spot; he wove together memories from several journeys to rebuild the mountain as a self-contained cosmos.
In the upper left corner you can find the title, four characters meaning a complete view of Mount Geumgang, followed by the painter's name and a small red seal.
The ambition of the whole picture is already written in its name.
Now let your eye travel along the ridge at the top.
The highest summit, Birobong, rises at the back, and its waters are said to flow down into Manpokdong, the valley at the centre, where they divide to left and right.
At the upper right, a poem praising the mountain is inscribed, so text and image work as one.
A line dating it to the winter of the gapin year gives us 1734, though some scholars believe the poem was added later by an owner of the painting.
Look at the jagged rock peaks on the right.
They are drawn in sharp vertical strokes, pulled swiftly up and down, to capture the split faces of granite.
Even the gaps between them are densely filled rather than left as empty mist.
Now turn to the earthen hills on the left.
Their soft forms are built from gentle ink dots, layer upon layer, so the wooded slopes look lush and welcoming.
Their dark ink stands clearly apart from the pale, bright rock.
Between these two worlds, a valley cuts down the middle of the picture.
A towering pillar of rock and, below it, a small roofed building keep watch over the deep gorge.
This is the seam where hard meets soft.
Down at the mouth of the valley, at the very bottom, you can spot a round arched bridge and a few small roofs.
This is the human doorway into the vast mountain, and the place where our own walk begins.
Step back, and the hard rock and the soft earth interlock in strong contrast.
This circular composition recalls the taegeuk, the union of yin and yang, and one scholar has even called it a Geumgang planet.
Jeong Seon painted around a hundred pictures of Geumgang, and this one, the largest, is considered his finest.
Turning away from Chinese models to paint Korea's real landscape, it is now a designated National Treasure.
The poem ends by saying that viewing this picture from your bedside is a joy to rival walking the mountain itself.
It is at once a landscape and a map of a worldview.
Standing here, which valley would you take into the mountain?
